sections.heading: Escaping Is How HTML Stays Honest
paragraphs: Rendering user-supplied or code-derived text safely requires escaping special characters like <, > and &. Encoding HTML prevents accidental execution and broken layouts across every page.
Escaping is security hygiene and rendering correctness in one step.
ChooseTools encodes and decodes HTML locally in your browser.
Without escaping, a single ampersand in a product description can break an entire page layout, turning meaningful content into browser error noise.

sections.heading: How to Escape HTML Entities
paragraphs: Safe text, instantly.
Paste raw text to escape <, >, &, quotes and other special characters into entities, or paste entity-laden HTML to decode back to readable text. Copy the version you need.
Processing is local, keeping your snippets confidential.
The bidirectional workflow means you can encode a snippet for safe embedding, and later decode the same block for human review without retyping anything.

sections.heading: Secure Display of User Input
paragraphs: Search results, message previews and comment rendering all need escaping to neutralize the dangerous characters users can type.
Escaped input renders as text, never as tags or scripts.
This one practice closes entire classes of injection surprises.
Cross-site scripting attacks rely on unescaped input reaching the DOM; consistent entity encoding neutralizes the attack vector before the browser ever interprets the string.

sections.heading: Literal Code Blocks and Documentation
paragraphs: Publishing code examples on a page means printing pre and code literally, which requires escaping the same characters being shown.
Encode your sample snippets to display them as text cleanly.
Documentation looks correct because entities render as visible characters.
Technical writers who escape code examples once and store the encoded version save hours of re-encoding when the documentation engine changes.

sections.heading: Common Entities and When to Use Them
paragraphs: The five core entities cover most cases: & for ampersand, < for less-than, > for greater-than, " for double quote, and ' for apostrophe.
Numeric character references handle non-ASCII symbols like em dashes, curly quotes and currency signs when the document encoding does not guarantee them.
Knowing which entities your output context requires prevents mojibake across email clients, CMS editors and plain-text renderers.

sections.heading: Double-Encoding: A Common Mistake
paragraphs: Applying HTML encoding twice turns & into &amp;, which displays the literal text ampersand instead of the intended symbol.
Developers encounter double-encoding when a CMS escapes content and then a template engine escapes it again.
Running a decode pass before re-encoding ensures the transformation is applied exactly once, preserving the intended output.

sections.heading: Two Directions, One Tool
paragraphs: Encode for safe output; decode to recover the readable original for auditing or editing.
Round trips preserve content exactly.
Both directions fit build and editorial work.
Developers use encoding in build pipelines to sanitize generated HTML, then use decoding to inspect the same output during code review.

paragraphs: HTML fragments from internal tools and test suites encode locally.
No upload, no account, no watermark — across every platform.
Web hygiene without exposure.
Internal dashboards and admin panels that handle sensitive user data benefit from local encoding because the snippets never pass through a third-party service.

sections.heading: Encoding in Email and Notification Templates
paragraphs: Email clients render HTML inconsistently, and unescaped special characters are a frequent cause of broken subject lines and blank message bodies.
Encoding the dynamic portions of an email template before merging content guarantees that user names, product titles and prices display as plain text rather than being misinterpreted.
Notification systems that escape dynamic fields reduce support tickets caused by garbled output across the many renderers in the wild.

faqs.q: Which characters does HTML encoding escape?
faqs.a: The special characters <, >, &, quotes and similar reserved symbols are translated into safe entities.

faqs.q: Can I decode entities back to readable HTML?
faqs.a: Yes. The tool works both ways, reconstructing the original text from encoded entities.
Yes. Everything runs locally in your browser with no uploads or accounts.

faqs.q: What is the difference between encoding and minification?
faqs.a: Encoding replaces special characters with safe entities to prevent rendering errors, while minification removes whitespace and comments to reduce file size. They serve different purposes in a web build.

faqs.q: What happens if I encode the same text twice?
faqs.a: Double-encoding produces incorrect output such as &amp; instead of &. The tool lets you decode first to ensure a single clean encoding pass.

faqs.q: Is HTML encoding the same as URL encoding?
faqs.a: No. HTML encoding converts HTML-reserved characters into entities for safe display, while URL encoding converts characters into percent-encoded values for safe inclusion in web addresses.

faqs.q: Do I need to escape apostrophes in single-quoted HTML attributes?
faqs.a: Yes. An apostrophe inside a single-quoted attribute value must be escaped as ' so the browser does not treat it as the closing quote.
